summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis. The age of consent is 14 years, applied equally regardless of gender or sexual orientation, with sex below that age treated as statutory rape.

State-level anti-discrimination protection is explicit. The Anti-Discrimination Law adopted in 2016 bans discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination had covered sexual orientation and gender expression but omitted gender identity as originally intended. The Sarajevo Open Centre presented the 2016 amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality after public consultations in late 2015.

Bias-motivated offences carry sentencing enhancement at entity level. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code in April 2016 to name sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances, published on 15 June 2016; Republika Srpska and Brčko District already had comparable provisions.

Public assembly has drawn organised violence. The Queer Sarajevo Festival in 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats; eight people, including a police officer, were injured, and in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that the authorities had failed to protect participants' freedom of assembly. In February 2014 Sarajevo Pride organisers were violently attacked even though they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier, and Human Rights Watch called for prosecution of the attackers. The first BiH Pride March was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers. In March 2023 police in Banja Luka cancelled LGBTQ film screenings citing security concerns, and activists were chased and attacked afterwards.

Social attitudes recorded in surveys are hostile. A 2015 survey found 48% of respondents would try to "cure" a child who came out as gay and 16% would stop communicating with that child; 19% supported granting same-sex couples some marriage-associated rights. A 2017 Pew poll found 13% support for same-sex marriage and 84% opposed.

No legal recognition of same-sex couples exists at national or entity level. The Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and households of same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex households. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has no route to partner recognition. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a request to legalise civil unions on 19 October 2018 and established a working group in January 2020, whose start was postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, the annual assessment by the leading local monitor, recorded a series of negative events with significant impact over the preceding year and described a long-visible worsening trend as increasingly evident.
tangentialFactors:
A 2017 PLOS ONE qualitative study documents the stigma and discrimination men who have sex with men report from healthcare professionals and from the wider community in Bosnia and Herzegovina, indicating that clinical settings are not reliably neutral for LGBTI patients.

A 2021 study found that the 2019 Sarajevo Pride parade increased support for LGBT activism in Sarajevo but not elsewhere in the country.
localsOnly: Legal gender recognition is formally available but vague and ineffective in practice. The Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions changes to identity documents on a "completed" medical transition, and the constraints are described as discriminatory and degrading. Legal gender change is available only after sex reassignment surgery and other medical treatments.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not document prosecutions or convictions under the entity-level hate-crime provisions, so the practical weight of those sentencing enhancements is unresolved.

The status of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina civil-union working group after its January 2020 postponement is not sourced.

The most recent public-attitude figures in the inventory are the 2015 survey and the 2017 Pew poll; no later national polling is recorded.
